common_name: General Jacqueminot Rose (Fragrant Crimson Hybrid Perpetual)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; introduced in France in 1853, General Jacqueminot became one of the most influential red roses of the 19th century.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Introduced in France in 1853, General Jacqueminot bears large, intensely fragrant, velvety crimson-red double blooms on a vigorous, upright shrub, and its rich color and powerful old-rose scent made it hugely influential as a parent behind countless later red roses, including many modern hybrid teas. It blooms mainly in a strong spring flush with some sporadic repeat later in the season, a typical pattern for Hybrid Perpetual roses bred before reliable everblooming traits were established. Prune back by about a third in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering canes.

common_name: Comte de Chambord Rose (Fragrant Repeat-Blooming Portland Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Comte de Chambord is a Portland rose introduced in 1860, valued for reliable repeat bloom unusual among old garden roses.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Comte de Chambord belongs to the Portland class of old garden roses, prized for combining strong old-rose fragrance and full, quartered deep pink blooms with genuine repeat flowering through the season, a trait most other old garden rose classes lack. The compact, upright shrub fits more easily into a mixed border than sprawling once-blooming antique roses, and its dense, informal double flowers make an excellent cut rose with exceptional scent. Prune back by about a third in late winter and deadhead spent blooms through the season to encourage continued flowering.

common_name: Baron Girod de l'Ain Rose (Red Petals Edged White Hybrid Perpetual)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this 1897 Hybrid Perpetual sport is known for its distinctive white-picotee-edged red petals.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. A sport discovered in 1897, Baron Girod de l'Ain bears large, fragrant, deep red double blooms each irregularly edged in a crisp band of white, a striking picotee effect that makes every flower distinct and has kept the cultivar sought after by old-rose collectors ever since. Like other Hybrid Perpetuals it blooms mainly in a strong spring flush with some sporadic repeat later in the season. Prune back by about a third in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering canes.

common_name: Jacques Cartier Rose (Fragrant Repeat-Blooming Portland Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Jacques Cartier is a Portland rose introduced in 1868, valued for reliable repeat bloom.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Jacques Cartier is a classic Portland rose bearing full, quartered, clear pink blooms with a strong, sweet fragrance, opening in a heavy spring flush and then continuing to repeat through summer and into fall, a genuine advantage over the many old garden rose classes that bloom only once. Its compact, upright habit suits a mixed border as readily as a dedicated antique rose garden. Prune back by about a third in late winter and deadhead spent blooms through the season to encourage continued flowering.

common_name: Sweet Drift Rose (Clear Pink Double Groundcover Rose)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Sweet Drift is part of the low-growing, spreading Drift groundcover rose series bred for continuous bloom and disease resistance.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun. Sweet Drift bears clear, soft pink, fully double flowers in dense clusters on a low, spreading, groundcover-type shrub, part of the Drift series bred by crossing miniature roses with groundcover roses to combine compact size with vigorous, disease-resistant, everblooming performance. Its low, mounding habit suits it to edging a border, cascading over a low wall, or massing as a flowering groundcover, and it blooms continuously from spring to frost with minimal deadheading required. Established plants tolerate heat and drought well and need little more than an annual light pruning in late winter to stay tidy.

common_name: Oso Easy Italian Ice Rose (Pink-and-Cream Bicolor Landscape Rose)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Oso Easy Italian Ice is part of a landscape rose series bred for disease resistance and low-maintenance repeat bloom.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun. Oso Easy Italian Ice bears unusual bicolor blooms opening pink and cream and shifting in tone as they age, so a single plant can show several shades at once, a distinctive novelty color pattern among landscape shrub roses. Bred for strong disease resistance and continuous bloom without deadheading, it fits low-maintenance foundation plantings and mixed borders where spraying and fussing over roses isn't practical. Established plants tolerate heat and drought well and need only an annual light pruning in late winter to stay compact and floriferous.

common_name: Dortmund Rose (Single Red-and-White Repeat-Blooming Climber)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, fence, or pillar; Dortmund is a Kordesii-class climber bred for cold hardiness and repeat bloom.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, fence, or pillar for the climbing canes to be trained onto. Dortmund bears large, single, bright red flowers with a bold white eye at the center and a light fragrance, opening in dramatic clusters against glossy, disease-resistant dark green foliage, and unlike many older climbers it reliably repeats its bloom through summer rather than flowering just once. As a Kordesii-class rose bred from cold-hardy species stock, it tolerates harsher winters than many climbing roses. Tie new canes horizontally along the support as they grow, since horizontal training encourages more flowering side shoots than canes left to grow straight up.

common_name: Rambling Rector Rose (Vigorous Creamy White Rambler)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun with a very sturdy support, such as a large tree or pergola, since Rambling Rector grows extremely large.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun, choosing a very sturdy support such as a mature tree, large pergola, or long fence, since Rambling Rector is among the most vigorous roses in cultivation and can climb 20 feet or more. Once each summer it produces a spectacular, single heavy flush of small, semi-double, creamy white, musk-scented flowers that smother the entire plant, followed by an equally showy display of small orange-red hips in fall that persist into winter. Because it blooms only once and grows so large, it suits an informal setting like scrambling into an old tree rather than a small, tended garden bed. Prune only to control size or remove dead wood, ideally right after the summer bloom.

common_name: Albertine Rose (Coppery Salmon-Pink Fragrant Rambler)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy fence, arbor, or pergola; introduced in 1921, Albertine is a once-blooming rambler prized for its intense fragrance.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy fence, arbor, or pergola. Introduced in France in 1921, Albertine produces an overwhelming single flush of double, coppery salmon-pink blooms each early summer, carrying an intense, sweet fragrance that made it one of the most beloved ramblers of the 20th century for training over cottage doorways and arbors. Reddish young canes and glossy foliage add interest even between the single, dramatic bloom period. Prune only to control size or remove dead and crossing wood right after the summer bloom, since it flowers on the previous year's growth.

common_name: Paul's Himalayan Musk Rose (Extremely Vigorous Blush-Pink Rambler)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun with an exceptionally sturdy, large support, such as a mature tree, since this rambler can grow 30 feet or more.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun, choosing an extremely sturdy, large support such as a mature tree, since Paul's Himalayan Musk is among the most rampant ramblers grown, capable of climbing 30 feet or more into a tree canopy. Once each early summer it produces a spectacular single flush of small, soft blush-pink, musk-scented double flowers borne in huge cascading clusters that can smother an entire tree in bloom. Because of its enormous ultimate size and single bloom season, it is best suited to a large property where it can be left to scramble freely rather than a small, formal garden. Prune only to control size or remove dead wood, ideally right after the summer bloom.

common_name: Veilchenblau Rose (Violet-Purple Streaked Rambler)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy fence or arbor; introduced in Germany in 1909, Veilchenblau is a once-blooming rambler grown for its unusual violet-purple color.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy fence or arbor, and note that it tolerates more shade than most roses, blooming reasonably well in partial shade. Introduced in Germany in 1909, Veilchenblau bears a single spring flush of small, semi-double flowers that open magenta-violet streaked with white and fade through smoky lavender-gray as they age, a genuinely unusual color range among roses that has earned it the nickname "blue rose" despite never being a true blue. Its thornless canes and light, sweet fragrance add to its appeal for training over an arbor or fence where visitors brush past. Prune only to control size or remove dead wood right after the summer bloom, since it flowers on the previous year's growth.

common_name: Dorothy Perkins Rose (Classic Rose-Pink Cluster-Flowered Rambler)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy fence or arbor; introduced in 1901, Dorothy Perkins was one of the most widely planted ramblers of the early 20th century.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy fence or arbor. Introduced in the United States in 1901, Dorothy Perkins produces enormous single-flush clusters of small, double, rose-pink flowers each summer, and became so widely planted in early 20th-century gardens that it remains one of the most historically iconic ramblers, though it is somewhat prone to powdery mildew compared to newer disease-resistant climbers. Its flexible, trailing canes make it well suited to training over an arch, pergola, or fence. Prune only to control size or remove dead wood right after the summer bloom, since it flowers on the previous year's growth.

common_name: American Pillar Rose (Vigorous Pink-and-White-Eyed Rambler)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy fence, arbor, or pergola; introduced in 1902, American Pillar is a vigorous once-blooming rambler.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy fence, arbor, or pergola. Introduced in 1902, American Pillar produces a spectacular single summer flush of large, single, deep pink flowers each marked with a bold white eye at the center, borne in such profusion that a mature plant in full bloom is hard to miss from a distance. Its vigorous growth and near-total lack of fragrance are typical of this class, but the sheer scale of the once-yearly floral display has kept it a garden favorite for well over a century. Prune only to control size or remove dead wood right after the summer bloom, since it flowers on the previous year's growth.

common_name: Rosa Mundi (Pink-and-White Striped Gallica Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Rosa Mundi is a centuries-old Gallica sport dating to at least the 16th century, blooming once in a single heavy spring flush.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Rosa Mundi tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough historic Gallica. Recorded since at least the 1500s, this striking sport of the Apothecary's Rose bears semi-double blooms irregularly striped and splashed in shades of pink, crimson, and white, no two flowers looking quite alike, on dense, compact, relatively thorny canes. Like other Gallicas it blooms just once, in a spectacular, fragrant flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Charles de Mills Rose (Deep Crimson-Purple Flat-Flowered Gallica)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Charles de Mills is a Gallica rose of uncertain but early origin, blooming once in a single heavy spring flush.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Charles de Mills tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough Gallica of uncertain but early origin. Its very full, densely packed double flowers open a rich crimson-purple and open remarkably flat with a neatly quartered, almost geometric center, considered by many collectors one of the most perfectly formed blooms of any old garden rose, carrying a strong, classic old-rose fragrance. Like other Gallicas it blooms just once, in a spectacular flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Tuscany Superb Rose (Dark Velvety Maroon-Purple Gallica)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Tuscany Superb is an improved 19th-century form of the historic Gallica rose Tuscany.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Tuscany Superb tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough 19th-century Gallica. An improved, larger-flowered form of the historic rose Tuscany, it bears dense, semi-double blooms in the darkest velvety maroon-purple of any Gallica, with prominent golden stamens providing striking contrast against the near-black petals, and a strong, classic old-rose fragrance. Like other Gallicas it blooms just once, in a spectacular flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Great Maiden's Blush Rose (Soft Blush-Pink Fragrant Alba Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Great Maiden's Blush is a centuries-old Alba rose famed for its subtle color and tolerance of light shade.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Alba roses like Great Maiden's Blush tolerate more shade than most roses, a legacy of their origin as tough, adaptable garden plants long predating modern breeding. Recorded since at least the 15th century, it bears intensely fragrant, soft blush-pink double blooms against distinctive gray-green foliage, a refined color combination that has earned it poetic nicknames across the centuries. Like other Albas it blooms just once, in a fragrant flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season, and it is exceptionally disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Alba Semi-Plena Rose (White Semi-Double Historic Alba Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Alba Semi-plena is one of the oldest garden roses still cultivated, historically grown for attar of roses production.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Alba roses tolerate more shade than most roses, a legacy of their origin as tough, adaptable garden plants. One of the oldest identifiable garden roses still in commerce, Alba Semi-plena bears fragrant, semi-double white flowers with prominent golden stamens against distinctive gray-green foliage, and was historically cultivated in quantity for attar of roses and rosewater production, most famously in Bulgaria's Rose Valley. Like other Albas it blooms just once, in a fragrant flush in late spring, followed by an attractive display of orange-red hips in fall. It is exceptionally disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Felicite Parmentier Rose (Pale Flesh-Pink Fragrant Alba Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; introduced in France in 1834, Felicite Parmentier is a compact Alba rose valued for its neat, dense habit.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Alba roses tolerate more shade than most roses, a legacy of their origin as tough, adaptable garden plants. Introduced in France in 1834, Felicite Parmentier bears very full, quartered, pale flesh-pink double blooms with a strong, sweet fragrance, opening from deeper pink buds on a notably compact, dense shrub, more manageable in size than many taller Alba roses. Like other Albas it blooms just once, in a fragrant flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season, and it is exceptionally disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Madame Hardy Rose (Pure White Green-Eyed Damask Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; introduced in France in 1832, Madame Hardy is considered one of the finest white Damask roses ever raised.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Madame Hardy tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough 19th-century Damask. Introduced in France in 1832, it bears exquisitely formed, pure white double blooms that open flat with a distinctive small green button eye at the center, a refined and much-admired detail that has made it a benchmark white old garden rose for nearly two centuries, carrying a fresh, lemony Damask fragrance. Like other Damasks it blooms just once, in a spectacular fragrant flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Ispahan Rose (Clear Pink Long-Blooming Damask Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Ispahan is a Damask rose of ancient Persian origin, notable for an unusually long bloom period among once-blooming old roses.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Ispahan tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough, ancient Damask. Believed to date back centuries to Persia, Ispahan bears clear pink, intensely fragrant double blooms and, while it still flowers just once a year rather than truly repeating, its single bloom period runs unusually long, six weeks or more, considerably longer than most other once-blooming old garden roses. Like other Damasks it needs only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering rather than the intensive spray programs modern roses often require, and it is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy.

common_name: Fantin-Latour Rose (Soft Pink Cupped Centifolia Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Fantin-Latour is a Centifolia-type rose named for the French painter famous for his rose still lifes.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Fantin-Latour tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough old garden rose. Named for the French painter Henri Fantin-Latour, celebrated for his luminous rose still-life paintings, this Centifolia-type rose bears very full, softly cupped, soft pink double blooms with a light, sweet fragrance on a graceful, arching, relatively tall shrub. Like other old Centifolia types it blooms just once, in a fragrant flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.
